top_choice_rationale: The optical lattice clock alone (Katori, Ye) is the most mature and cleanly attributed achievement on the slate. The magic-wavelength lattice lets an ensemble of neutral atoms be interrogated without Doppler, recoil or light-shift penalties, which neither the 2005 comb prize nor the 2012 single-quantum-system prize credited. The 1e-18 performance is reproduced across Sr, Yb and Hg clocks and by inter-laboratory comparisons, and it has already delivered centimetre-scale gravitational redshift and tighter bounds on drifting constants. The two names map onto the concept (Katori) and the demonstrated accuracy and many-body physics (Ye). Adding a one-name IceCube part (P002) dilutes it with a credit I cannot defend, so I rank it below twisted bilayer graphene, which I would accept with a citation limited to the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated states. Topological insulators (P004) are mature but carry the 2016 overlap and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap. All proposals still rank above no award.
recusal_note: Possible connection: my doctoral-period research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder; Ye is associated with the JILA environment around Hall, though my profile documents no tie to Katori or Ye. My atomic-physics and laser-spectroscopy background is also close to the field of B043. Flagged for the chair; ballot completed regardless.
